node.label: Leanne Betasamosake Simpson
node.date_label: Dancing on Our Turtle’s Back (2011) · Land as Pedagogy (2014) · As We Have Always Done (2017)
node.description: Simpson argues that Indigenous resurgence must build political alternatives to settler rule rather than seek inclusion within it. As We Have Always Done (2017) connects resistance to land dispossession with opposition to capitalist exploitation, white supremacy and heteropatriarchy. Dancing on Our Turtle’s Back (2011) had already argued that reconciliation requires political resurgence. “Land as Pedagogy” (2014) turns this programme toward the authority of Indigenous intellectual work. Tiffany Lethabo King’s 2023 review values the book’s significance for Black feminist and queer scholarship and Indigenous–Black alliances.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Dancing on Our Turtle’s Back (2011); “Land as Pedagogy” (2014); “Grounded Normativity / Place-Based Solidarity,” with Glen Coulthard (2016); As We Have Always Done (2017).
node.scope_note: Selected primary passages of the 2001 and 2014 articles read; the 2016 coauthored article is identified bibliographically only. The 2011 book is known through its publisher and catalogue; the 2017 book through its publisher and King’s 2023 review, not a full primary reading. Gravlin’s criticism is known only from its title; the article is unread. Deloria’s 2001 chapter, Audra Simpson’s 2014 book and Roediger’s address remain unread here.

proposed_edges.relationship: Simpson and Coulthard coauthored “Grounded Normativity / Place-Based Solidarity” (American Quarterly, 2016).
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Byline; pp. 249–250, 254–255, read. Joint voice: “we are calling”. Coulthard’s separately marked autobiographical argument is not Simpson’s.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Land as Pedagogy” (2014), Leanne Betasamosake Simpson invokes Audra Simpson’s Mohawk Interruptus (2014) for the politics of refusal.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: P. 22, n. 41: “politics of refusal”; bibliography p. 25. Selected article passages read; Mohawk Interruptus unread here. Specific resource, not sole derivation.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Land as Pedagogy” (2014) cites Deloria’s “Traditional Technology” (2001) to support education grounded in Indigenous contexts and processes.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: P. 9 cites Deloria pp. 58–60; reference p. 24. “Indigenous context” is methodological framing; Deloria’s chapter itself remains unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Land as Pedagogy” (2014) develops resurgence as an Indigenous intellectual and political project exceeding inclusion in existing academic institutions.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: P. 22: “resurgence of Indigenous intellectual systems”. Selected article passages read; earlier book unread. No account of community teachings proposed.

proposed_edges.relationship: As We Have Always Done (2017) advances Indigenous resurgence as refusal of dispossession and an alternative to the settler state’s organizing logics.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Publisher Description and eBook metadata read; original date 17 October 2017, paperback 2020. Book body unread; no criticism of a particular settler-colonial scholar inferred.

proposed_edges.relationship: “Aboriginal Peoples and Knowledge” (2001) argues that research direction belongs to Elders and community experts, rather than being secured by participatory methods alone.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Pp. 140–142, especially p. 142: “control and direction of the work”. Publisher PDF read selectively; methodological claim only, without community-knowledge content.

proposed_edges.relationship: According to Tiffany Lethabo King, As We Have Always Done (2017) historicizes colonial gender violence through missions, schooling and white women’s enforcement of the Indian Act.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: King 2023, p. 184, discussion of chapter 7, citing book p. 97: “gendered analysis”. Review read; book chapter unread. Contribution is mediated by this named reader.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her closing essay for ActiveHistory.ca's January 2016 Indigenous theme week, Mary Jane Logan McCallum cites Leanne Simpson's and Billy-Ray Belcourt's posts from that week as identifying work still to be done beyond curriculum reform such as Winnipeg's Indigenous Course Requirement.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: The concluding body paragraph explicitly uses their critiques in evaluating curriculum reform; the opening collective thanks is not the evidence. No wider intellectual debt is claimed.

proposed_edges.relationship: In As We Have Always Done (2017), Simpson challenges the treatment of queer life as new to Indigenous societies and argues for its normalization within Indigenous life, as Tiffany Lethabo King explains in her 2023 review.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: King’s substantive discussion of chapter 8 supports this contribution to sexuality and queer history. Evidence is the review; the book was not independently read. No narrative or ceremonial content is used.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 2022 review essay on Chakrabarty's The Climate of History in a Planetary Age, Brooke Ackerly names Simpson's account of Nishnaabeg methodologies, citing Dancing on Our Turtle's Back (2011), as a resource for understanding the planetary age without constructing binaries.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Ackerly names Simpson in the body and identifies both books in note 5. This records her assessment of a methodological contribution to climate history; it does not establish Chakrabarty’s reception of Simpson.
